# Operator Payload Troubleshooting Tree

When a report of inconsistent operator payload results arrives, the first step is not to assign blame to AESGCM or staging. The two object names currently retained point to the staging lifecycle and the serialization boundary, respectively; they may appear near the same call, or they may simply be two points to check in the same report.

The early records retained only `lmcache/v1/distributed/api.py` as an entry point, along with a to-do to add the actual calls. Later review still did not confirm that file as the staging container or the location of the serialization implementation. It is suitable for finding adjacent references, starting with interface objects and object key conversion; it is not suitable as a substitute for the caller explaining where the payload actually passed through.

First, collect what is already in the report: the result the user saw, the corresponding call entry point, the trigger sequence, and the attached sample. Having a sample does not mean the path has been located; it only means there is material available for further checking. If the submission contains only a result and no entry point, register it as “inconsistent results, call undetermined”, and do not break the issue down into a seemingly complete lifecycle.

```text
Inconsistent payload results
|
+-- Can the call locations before and after entering staging be identified?
|   |
|   +-- Yes
|   |   +-- Record the object representation held at each of the two locations
|   |   +-- The difference already appears before entering staging
|   |   |   `-- Stop assessing staging and return to the caller that constructs the payload
|   |   `-- The difference appears only after the confirmed staging boundary
|   |       `-- Retain that boundary and continue confirming the subsequent consumption location
|   |
|   `-- No
|       `-- Retain the sample and trigger sequence; staging remains unconfirmed
|
`-- Can the carriers before and after serialization be identified?
    |
    +-- Yes
    |   +-- Check operator AESGCM payload serialization separately
    |   `-- Record the object key representation and payload contents separately
    |
    `-- No
        `-- Request an interface compatibility entry point; do not infer the serialization location from the adjacent API file
```

## First distinguish the “differences” in the report

The differences in the report may be in the payload contents, the object key representation, or the result displayed by the caller. All three can make users see an inconsistency, but they lead to different entry points for further investigation. When recording them, first state clearly which one is being compared, to avoid mistakenly recording a text change in the object key as a payload rewrite.

If the report contains only object keys, first check the adjacent references around `to_encoded_object_key` and `to_object_key`. They are clues to object key conversion, not evidence of the payload lifecycle. If only the key's representation differs before and after conversion, and there are no locations at which to compare the payload, this record cannot be used to assess staging or treated as a AESGCM serialization anomaly.

Conversely, if object key conversion is not near the actual call, there is no need to include it in the investigation path just for completeness. The two names are retained here so that anyone looking back through the interface file can distinguish key conversion from the payload itself. The entry point provided by the caller takes priority over adjacent declarations guessed from keywords.

The trigger sequence also needs to be preserved as provided. At a minimum, it can indicate whether the report was raised before entering staging, at the handoff after staging, or when the caller read the result. An incomplete sequence does not invalidate the report; it simply cannot be used to determine the first location where the difference appeared. Do not replace gaps in the original record with another section of calls added later.

## Staging track: confirm only boundaries that have been observed

The operator payload staging lifecycle branch handles only the boundaries where an object enters staging, is in staging, and leaves staging. Before starting, there must be before-and-after locations that the caller can identify. Without these two locations, there are no objects to compare and no reason to call the report a staging anomaly.

When locations are available, first record the object representation before entering staging, then record the object representation after leaving staging. There is no requirement here to fabricate a seemingly identical intermediate payload; a newly created copy cannot show whether an object was replaced along the user's path. The record should identify which call location each side comes from, rather than merely saying “before” and “after”.

If the difference already appears before entering staging, stop attributing it to staging. What is known at this point is that the objects are inconsistent before the caller hands them to staging, so the next step should return to the call that constructs or passes the object. Do not keep asking `api.py` to explain the content change, and do not assume that staging internals still need to bear the same assessment just because the issue name contains lifecycle.

If the two available locations appear consistent but the user's result is still different, the only conclusion is: the sample has not placed the difference at the confirmed staging boundary. This does not establish that the staging path has no problem. Retain the unconfirmed calls between leaving staging and reading the result, and work backward from the consumption location corresponding to the user's result to fill them in.

The same report may contain more than one call entry point. Record them separately until the reference relationships can confirm that they really lead to the same staging location. Do not use a sample obtained from one entry point as a substitute for another; there is currently no material showing that this lifecycle has only one linear path.

The stopping conditions for this track are simple: the locations before and after staging cannot be identified, or the difference already exists before entering staging. The former lacks a call entry point, and the latter is already outside the staging boundary. Preserve both situations as they are, without recording them as a root cause found.

## Serialization track: establish the before-and-after carriers before discussing AESGCM

operator AESGCM payload serialization is module behavior to be checked, not a confirmed fault conclusion. Before entering this branch, it must be possible to identify which side holds the payload before and after serialization. Without the before-and-after carriers, it is impossible to distinguish whether the contents were already different before the handoff or whether the caller reads the same result differently on the receiving side.

Once the carriers are clear, record three local facts: the call location on the before side, the call location on the after side, and which side supplies the result the user sees. If object key conversion occurs in between, list it separately as well. This prevents changes in key representation from being mixed into payload content comparisons during later checks.

Do not expand the name AESGCM into keys, algorithm steps, or specific failure modes. This page has no such material. If the caller cannot provide the serialization location, the current action is to ask the interface compatibility maintainer for an entry point that can be inspected further; after obtaining it, confirm that it is a call the user actually went through, rather than one with a merely similar name.

If the difference can already be observed before serialization, stop at that fact and do not record AESGCM as the cause. If only the result read after serialization is available and the before-side carrier is missing, stop as well; what is missing is an object for comparison, not an answer that can be supplied by an interface file. After the interface compatibility maintainer confirms the entry point, add only the relationship between that entry point and the sample, without replacing the original report's trigger sequence.

## How to use the API file

The direct dependencies of `lmcache/v1/distributed/api.py` include `dataclass`, `enum`, `torch`, and logging initialization `init_logger`. It provides local navigation on the interface side. During inspection, first check whether the reported entry point touches object key conversion, then examine the interface objects that can be confirmed; do not infer the payload producer, staging container, or encryption processing point from these imports.

`to_encoded_object_key` and `to_object_key` should be included in the record only when the report involves object key representation. If the caller can explain that the same payload is unchanged before and after conversion and only the key text differs, separate that phenomenon from the payload anomaly. If the caller did not pass near these names, there is also no need to add a hypothetical key conversion path.

The interface file's role ends here: providing traceable adjacent declarations and object key clues. The actual calls are determined by the reported entry point. Newly added calls can still be valid material for checking staging or serialization even if they are not connected to this file.

## Unfinished parts of the cards

RCP-214 records inconsistent operator payload results in the user's environment. The card already has a sample, but the open item remains: continue only the current section, and do not mark the lifecycle as confirmed just because a sample is attached. Use the sample in the branches above, rather than as proof of which component owns the implementation.

RCP-216 lists operator AESGCM payload serialization separately and asks the corresponding module maintainer to check the current behavior and subsequent entry points. This item was later transferred to the interface compatibility maintainer, indicating that the first thing to clarify at the time was the inspection entry point. It does not mean that `api.py` is already responsible for serialization, nor does it mean that the phenomenon in RCP-214 has already been localized to AESGCM.

When both cards have usable content, RCP-214 brings back the report and sample, while RCP-216 brings back a module entry point for further inspection. Put the two into the same record only if the entry point really belongs to the call for that sample. If either is missing, continue to keep the two tracks separate.

At handoff, recording four items is enough: the result the user saw, the call entry point corresponding to the sample, the last confirmed staging boundary, and whether the carriers before and after serialization have been identified. If the last item is still missing, write “serialization boundary not found” directly. This lets the person taking over continue investigating from the missing location, rather than treating a generic payload description as a localization result.

# Webhook Build Migration Procedure

This round of checks covers two related changes that should not be treated as one: webhook init-container builders still organize the injection content associated with init containers; dynamic webhook argument removal removes arguments dynamically added to the webhook along the call chain. Keep these two paths separate during migration so that you can tell whether an issue comes from a change in builder output or from old arguments still being supplied by callers.

The entry point remains at `operator/internal/webhook/cacheblend_inject_builders.go`. The file belongs to the `webhook` package. Start with the imports at the top of the file and the objects adjacent to the builder; do not expand the first check to cache objects, runtime components, or other injection mechanisms. The checks here are whether callers still consume the content produced by the builder and whether they continue to add dynamic arguments after receiving it.

## Inventory the Old Calls First

Before migrating, record two aspects of each call site rather than doing a global replacement based only on function names.

- Does the builder participate in generating init-container? If so, record whether the caller receives the complete injection result or only part of it.
- Does the caller add request-specific webhook arguments before or after the builder? Even when argument names look similar, distinguish static configuration, existing-object handling, and dynamic assembly.
- Does the output still include mounts, existing objects, or init containers? Being in the same injection result as dynamic arguments does not mean they should be removed together.

A single call site may use both the builder and argument assembly. In that case, keep two check results: one stating whether the builder's result is still present, and another stating whether dynamic arguments have been removed from the webhook input. Recording only “injection works” can miss leftover arguments; recording only “arguments removed” can hide cases where init-container was skipped.

If you can see a builder call but cannot see where the arguments come from, mark it for follow-up. Do not record the absence of explicit arguments as completed removal: an outer object may supply them. Conversely, even if a caller no longer passes arguments, check whether it still consumes the builder's output.

## Order of Changes

First, hold the builder side steady. Confirm that init containers and their adjacent injection content are still organized through the existing builders path; do not also reorder unrelated mounts or existing-object handling in this round. This provides a comparable build baseline if differences appear later.

Second, remove dynamic webhook argument assembly at each caller. What is being removed is the calling convention for passing dynamic arguments, not by rewriting those arguments into the static content of init-container. If only the container, field, or wrapper layer has changed, the webhook may still receive the same information; that does not count as complete.

Third, review the combined result after the call. Check that the builder is still called, that init-container still enters the final injection result, and that dynamic arguments have not reappeared from another layer. Checking callers one by one is safer than a single replacement here, because builders are a shared entry point while argument assembly may remain in each caller's calling convention.

Fourth, leave a minimal before-and-after record. For each affected entry point, record only whether dynamic arguments existed before the change, whether it used the builder, and which initialization injection content was retained after the change. The comparison should support later review; there is no need to copy the entire webhook configuration into the record.

## Completion Criteria and Stop Points

The following do not, by themselves, mean the migration is complete: init-container still exists, but the caller or an upper-level wrapper still passes old arguments; dynamic arguments are gone, but the caller also bypasses the builder; or containers remain in the output, but adjacent content originally organized by the builder has been lost.

If any of these occur, stop at the call boundary rather than expanding the scope of changes. Check which object receives the builder output, then check whether arguments are still assembled after that object. If both places have changed, first record them as separate build-side and caller-side differences. Avoid replacing both paths in one fix and losing the basis for comparison.

Two boundaries still need confirmation: whether all existing callers share the same set of builders, and whether dynamic webhook argument removal only changes the arguments passed by callers or also affects the init-container content formed by the builder. Until these two questions are resolved, the migration record covers only the webhook injection paths that have been checked.

## Restore the Old Path

If a compatibility issue occurs, restore the affected caller rather than rolling back the whole group. First restore that call site's original dynamic argument assembly, then check whether the builder still generates the original initialization injection content. If init-container or adjacent content is still inconsistent after restoring the arguments, keep the issue scoped to the builder output or where it is consumed; do not continue attributing it to argument removal.

If the issue first appears on the builder side, first restore how that call site consumes the existing builder result. Keep dynamic arguments removed unless they have been confirmed to be an old calling convention required for recovery. After restoration, compare the minimal sample again: containers and adjacent injection content should return to their pre-change form, and dynamic arguments should appear only on old paths where they are genuinely needed.

To add: complete the caller list from actual references to `cacheblend_inject_builders.go`, and mark for each whether argument assembly happens before or after the builder.

# Multiprocess Bridge and Allocator Proposal

The first draft put the two topics side by side because they entered interface review at the same time; after rechecking, we still won't combine them into one commit. The timeout bridge handles visible results after a call completes, while the allocator split handles changes in check placement. If we bundle them, a failure will make it hard to quickly tell whether to revisit the observation output or the check move.

`lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/lmcache_driven_transfer.py` remains the nearby starting point for this round. The file header directly contains `dataclass`, `islice`, `Generator`, `Sequence`, and `threading`. Their proximity shows that data objects, iteration slices, and threads are involved here, but the file location is not proof of where allocator or timeout handling belongs. Start the recheck from this path, then confirm the relationships through actual references; don't assume new module names in the proposal.

## Keep the two small experiments first

The bridge candidate is to leave a narrow timeout observation output near the multiprocess call. This output only preserves the visible difference between one successful call and one failed call. It does not reorder the transfer flow or put allocator checks into the recording logic. This leaves an unresolved read question: does the caller read it on return, or does another observer read it? Don't settle this interface yet; first avoid expanding the bridge's responsibilities just to make reading easier.

Another candidate is to wrap timeout, thread state, and allocator checks together. We are not adopting that proposal at this stage. It appears to have only one entry point, but it would actually make a single check carry two kinds of changes: call observation and memory checking. If a failed call does not leave the expected difference, we would not know whether the wrapper failed to pass the result through or whether moving the check changed the call order. For this round, fewer entry points are not the highest-priority benefit.

Limit the allocator work to confirming execution of the existing checks first. Reproduction must start from the pre-call state; after completing the checks, observe whether any additional visible changes appear. Do not prescribe the extracted module's interface in advance, or make the bridge's new records a condition for the checks to be valid. If the checks can only complete by relying on the new records, the boundaries have not been separated yet; roll back this attempt to combine them and restore independent validation first.

## What to look at during the recheck

The observation when RCP-209 was created was that the actual multiprocess entry point did not match the sample results. It later entered the `release_classified` state and can serve as the starting point for the bridge recheck. The recheck samples should retain the results of one successful call and one failed call separately; “the call did not report an error” cannot replace distinguishing those two results. If the two output types end up identical, first record where the difference disappears rather than interpreting it as a side effect of the allocator split.

The observation when RCP-210 was created was confirmation of execution of the memory allocator module's existing checks. This starting point is only for the second item: capture the pre-call state, complete the checks, then look for any additional changes. If an additional change cannot be attributed to the moved check itself, pause the split rather than treating it as a normal effect of the bridge. The two cards each cover their own recheck direction; they do not share acceptance criteria at this stage.

## Sequence after review

1. Connect the timeout observation output first and retain both successful and failed samples.
2. Move the allocator checks independently, without changing the transfer call pattern.
3. Once the two items can be rechecked independently, discuss whether they need a shared record format.

Handle rollbacks independently too. If the bridge cannot keep success and failure distinguishable, roll back only the new observation output; if the allocator split causes unexplained additional changes, restore the checks to their original location. Rolling back one direction does not automatically invalidate results already obtained in the other.

Still undecided are the read entry point for timeout records and whether the extracted allocator checks need a separate caller contract. Another practical gap: no one has yet been named to read the success and failure samples over the long term. Leave these questions open rather than documenting the temporary observation output as a stable interface.

# Multi-backend device compatibility troubleshooting tree

The initial reports fell into two categories: only one device backend was discovered at runtime, or old call sites still fetched objects from the original location after DeviceInfo moved. The two issues were handled together at the time because the registry file both loads subclass packages at runtime and adds available entries to the factory.

Don't start with type annotations. `from __future__ import annotations`, `Any`, `Callable`, `Dict`, and `threading` at the top of `lmcache/v1/platform/_registry.py` only indicate deferred resolution, callback types, and proximity to concurrency code; they don't tell us which backends have been discovered.

Provisional troubleshooting order:

```text
A device is missing or an old import fails
├─ First distinguish: is a backend missing, or is the old location of DeviceInfo no longer valid?
├─ Backend missing: check whether the subclass packages have been loaded at runtime and have populated the factory
├─ Old location no longer valid: retain the call site and the object shape it expects
└─ Neither is clear: don't treat relocation as a registration failure
```

The earlier idea was that the registry could also cover all old calls after relocation. There are no counterexamples to this idea yet, but there isn't enough evidence to write it up as a recovery action either.

# Multi-Backend Device Compatibility Troubleshooting Tree

This record still starts from the same entry point: someone reports that multi-backend devices are not appearing where expected, or that an existing call no longer connects after DeviceInfo relocation. The previous version collapsed both into a single “registry not updated” issue, which was not sufficient during the actual review. Registration and relocation can both touch `_registry.py`, but they leave different clues when they fail.

The file’s old responsibility was described as: load at runtime the package containing those subclasses and populate the factory. The focus here is runtime loading and the factory; not every import failure should be fixed here. The adjacency of `annotations`, `Any`, `Callable`, `Dict` and `threading` remains at the top of the file. During review, it can be used to confirm that this is the old registration entry point, but not to infer the implementation status of a particular device backend.

After RCP-211 were added to the navigation, one multi-backend device discovery registry item in the record was still unconfirmed. That card is suitable for recording the version where the change first appeared and uncovered paths; it is not a substitute for live triage. RCP-212 are used to trace a caller that still uses DeviceInfo relocation compatibility: first check the version it actually depends on, then where it gets the object from, and finally record the current result. The two cards address different problems. Their conclusions must not be merged just because both contain the word device.

## Live Triage

```text
Symptom: device selection is abnormal, or an old call site cannot find DeviceInfo
│
├─ A. The report is that candidate backends were not discovered
│  ├─ Record the set of backends seen in the fixed reproduction; do not record only “multi-backend failure”
│  ├─ In the old revision, check whether the subclass package participated in runtime loading
│  ├─ Then check whether the factory received candidates after that path
│  └─ If the relationship between the subclass package and the factory is not yet confirmed, stop at RCP-211
│
├─ B. Candidate backends are present, but the old call still depends on the pre-relocation DeviceInfo
│  ├─ Record the call site, the old location it references, and the intended use of the object
│  ├─ Distinguish whether the import location changed or the object itself is no longer usable
│  └─ Hand off to RCP-212 to continue checking the caller’s version and entry point
│
└─ C. Both A and B are present
   ├─ Do not change the caller first to mask the discovery issue
   ├─ Do not add a compatibility alias to the registry to mask the relocation issue
   └─ Record the two observations separately, then decide whether they have a common cause
```

Here, “candidate backends are present” only means that the person investigating saw candidates on their own path; it does not mean that all backends are available. Conversely, an old call failure does not automatically prove that the factory was not populated. This distinction was not clearly documented before, so some people investigated imports first while others investigated discovery first, and neither side left a comparable record.

## Legacy Recovery Action

It was once recommended that, when an old location failed, a compatibility layer should first be added at the registry, followed by confirmation of backend discovery. This was intended to let the old call continue as quickly as possible, but it assumed that DeviceInfo relocation was only a change to the registry’s outer layer. Keep this recommendation as historical reference, but no longer treat it as the default action: it mixes the caller’s old reference with missing factory candidates, making it difficult to determine which part actually changed the result.

The safer approach is to first state clearly whether the error occurred in A, B or C. A records only the relationship between runtime loading and the factory; B records only the relationship between the old call site and the relocation. If both must actually be changed, the record should explicitly state that they are two actions in the same reproduction, rather than writing the second as an inevitable result of the first.

## Materials for On-Call

- The combination of device backends in the triggering scenario;
- The actual registration entry reached and the revision used at the time;
- For A, observations about the subclass package and the factory;
- For B, the old call site, old location and object usage;
- For C, the independent results for A and B.

Do not leave only “registry issue” or “compatibility regression.” On this page, those two terms point to different troubleshooting branches. The unconfirmed items in RCP-211 are still unresolved; the caller check in RCP-212 also cannot be performed on its behalf by this page.

versions.body:
# Multi-Backend Device Compatibility Troubleshooting Tree

This page preserves the troubleshooting approach used around the old registration entry point. It is often treated as a shortcut for “the device was not recognized,” but the original issue actually spanned two adjacent boundaries: multi-backend device discovery and DeviceInfo relocation compatibility. Both appeared during the same period of changes, and both could lead people to `lmcache/v1/platform/_registry.py`; treating them as the same failure was the earliest misjudgment recorded on this page.

Start with a rough classification of the reported behavior. If the caller cannot obtain the expected backend from the outset, look at discovery first. If candidates already appear, but an old call still uses DeviceInfo at its pre-relocation location or in its pre-relocation shape, look at relocation first. Record it as a mixed case only if the same reproduction actually shows both symptoms. Do not jump straight to a mixed case just because both platform and device appear in the logs.

The old file description identifies `_registry.py` as the place that loads the packages containing subclasses at runtime and populates the factory. This description is still a useful signpost when tracing back from symptoms. It explains why “the file can be imported” is no substitute for confirming that “the candidates have entered the factory”: the former only proves that the investigator has reached a Python entry point, while the latter is closer to what the discovery branch is concerned with.

The `from __future__ import annotations`, `Any`, `Callable`, `Dict` and `threading` at the top of the file are also still kept alongside the checklist. They help confirm which old entry point is being examined and the implementation conventions around it; they are not a device capability table. Someone once saw `Callable` and attributed the failure to an unregistered callback, then saw `threading` and suspected initialization order; neither led to a reusable assessment. Without corresponding observations of subclass loading and factory state, these imports should not be used to draw conclusions about backend discovery.

## First Ask What Is Actually Missing

At the start of troubleshooting, collecting just two statements is enough: which backend the caller wants; and whether what it actually gets is “no candidates,” an unsuitable candidate, or a call site still referencing the old DeviceInfo. There is no need to determine the root cause first. Instead, avoid recasting “no candidates” and “the object cannot be found at the old location” as the same thing.

```text
Device-related exception
│
├─ The expected backend is missing from the report
│  │
│  ├─ Capture the triggering path and the candidate set observed at the time
│  ├─ Check whether the subclass packages entered the old registration flow at runtime
│  ├─ Check whether the factory has the corresponding candidates after that path runs
│  ├─ Evidence is missing for either step: record discovery as unconfirmed
│  └─ Both steps check out, but the call still fails: investigate the caller's selection criteria
│
├─ Candidates exist, but the old call site still accesses the old location of DeviceInfo
│  │
│  ├─ Record the old location, the call site and what the object is used for
│  ├─ Check “import location changed” and “object semantics changed” separately
│  ├─ Only the old location is missing: continue along the relocation track
│  ├─ The object's use has also changed: do not add speculative compatibility in the registry
│  └─ The caller's version is unknown: stop at caller verification
│
└─ Both symptoms occur together
   │
   ├─ First separate them into discovery observations and relocation observations
   ├─ Do not treat adding an alias as evidence that the discovery issue has recovered
   ├─ Do not treat missing factory entries as evidence that an old import failed
   └─ Save each set separately before assessing whether there is a shared change
```

The stopping points in this tree matter more than “fixing it until it runs.” In one old record, a compatibility layer for DeviceInfo was inserted early into the registration path. On the surface, this allowed an old call to proceed, but it did not answer whether the target backend had actually entered the factory. In retrospect, the same patch both concealed a discovery gap and allowed the caller to keep depending on the object's pre-relocation location. That action is marked as deprecated here: this does not mean that no compatibility layer should exist, but that it cannot be the default recovery method while the discovery branch remains unresolved.

## Discovery Track: Preserve What Can Be Compared

When a report says “only one of the multiple backends is recognized,” the old approach often jumped straight to “is the registry broken?” That question is too broad. First preserve the backend combination that triggered the behavior and the candidate set that actually appeared; then pursue only two local questions: whether the relevant subclass packages were loaded at runtime, and whether the factory had the corresponding candidates afterward. If there is no evidence for the first, do not point directly to the factory; if there is no evidence for the second, do not recast the issue as subclasses not being loaded either.

The reason for writing it this way is not to make troubleshooting records longer, but that the old entry point already placed runtime loading and the factory within closely related responsibilities. If the report leaves only “the registry does not support multiple backends,” the next investigator cannot tell whether this means the packages were not loaded, the factory did not receive entries, or the caller simply never retrieved the correct candidates.

RCP-211 is used to keep user paths not yet covered by this track and checks of the first version in which behavior changed. The card's history still contains one unconfirmed item, so this page cannot present discovery as a completed compatibility commitment. When escalation is needed, include the actual triggering path, the candidate set, and whether each of the two local observations above is available; do not just forward the words “multi-backend device discovery registry.”

A common but unhelpful shortcut is to draw a conclusion about a backend based on the old registry path first. The path can lead people back to the old entry point, but it provides no evidence that the backend has been selected or is usable. If the observation goes only as far as “candidates are missing,” stop the record at missing candidates; if it goes only as far as “subclass packages are unconfirmed,” stop the record at unconfirmed runtime loading. Both stopping points are more useful for later comparison than collapsing the unknowns into a single fix.

## Relocation Track: First Reconstruct What the Old Call Expected

Checks for DeviceInfo relocation compatibility start with the caller, not the registry. Preserve three pieces of local evidence: the object location referenced by the old call, the object's use that it depends on, and the version the caller is actually using. If the old location no longer works but the object's use has not changed, the issue may still be only a migration omission; if the object's shape or use expected by the caller has changed, it cannot be called simple relocation.

RCP-212 is the navigation point for this track. It calls for finding a caller that still uses the old compatibility path and checking its version, entry point and current result. Here, “current result” refers only to the result of checking that caller. It does not represent all callers, nor does it mean the registry's discovery has been verified. The places where the old page described “the call still works” as “device registration has recovered” have now been corrected: the former may mean only that compatibility for the old location is temporarily provided, while the latter still requires observations from the discovery track itself.

When an old call needs to be allowed to continue temporarily, the temporary action should still first be recorded under the relocation track. Do not place it alongside factory initialization, and do not use it to overwrite the original call site. This preserves a fact for later troubleshooting: the call once depended on the pre-relocation location. If the compatibility action changes the object's use or introduces a new entry point, keep a separate migration record for the caller; this page does not decide its migration strategy for it.

## Old Assessment and Correction

**Old assessment, retained:** As long as `_registry.py` can load subclass packages at runtime, the registry should also absorb DeviceInfo relocation; discovery and compatibility can therefore be handled with the same recovery action.

This assessment came from the early habit of grouping the two symptoms under one issue. At the time, the candidate set, factory state and old call sites were not recorded separately, so it seemed convenient. The danger is that a compatibility alias may stop an old call from reporting an error without supplying the missing candidates; conversely, candidates appearing in the factory cannot automatically make a call that still references an old location correct.

**Correction added later:** The most recent field feedback prompted us to withdraw the default claim that “the registry can take care of all old calls along the way.” The registry is now treated only as one entry point for tracing discovery; whether old calls to DeviceInfo need compatibility must be confirmed separately based on the caller's version, entry point and use of the object. This correction has not resolved the unconfirmed paths in RCP-211, nor has it identified all adopters for RCP-212.

The old paragraph has not been deleted because it still explains why someone might merge the two branches. New troubleshooting records should explicitly identify themselves as discovery, relocation or mixed cases. A mixed case does not mean the two share a root cause either; it only means that the same reproduction contains two sets of observations that still need to be compared.

## What to Write for Handoff

For the discovery branch, leave at least: the triggering path, the expected and actual candidate sets, observations of runtime subclass loading, and whether the factory has entries. For the relocation branch, leave at least: the old call site, the old location, the object's use and the caller's version. When evidence is insufficient, write only “which item lacks evidence,” without stretching that into a claim that the backend is unsupported or migration is complete.

If someone reports that “both branches are unstable,” first ask whether this really occurs in the same call path. One symptom in each of two different environments should not be combined into a single incident. If both occur in the same path, still separate them according to the tree first: record the discovery branch's candidate set, then record the reference at the old call site. Only after completing these two records is there a basis for comparing whether they share a change.

This page remains troubleshooting material around the old entry point and should not replace a caller compatibility checklist. RCP-211 is reserved for unconfirmed discovery paths, and RCP-212 is reserved for callers still using the old location of DeviceInfo. The old recovery action can help explain the history, but is no longer the default treatment.

versions.body:
# History of Cache Event Publication

This record preserves the assessments of cache event boundaries made during Q3. The initial draft treated `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/blend_v3.py` as the common point for collection, publication, sequence admission, and eviction; that description was later used in integration troubleshooting and was therefore not deleted. It came from queue dependencies visible near the file and the trade-off at the time of wanting fewer entry points, not from a complete verification of responsibilities.

In retrospect, the presence of `dataclass`, `Queue`, and `QueueEmpty` in the file only shows that the nearby components provide the conditions for organizing batches of objects. Yet the initial draft turned “can hold a queue” into “owns the event protocol,” and also folded directory updates into the same chain. This is the part of this page most likely to mislead later readers: if an old script cannot find the consumer or eviction component along this path, that does not mean no event was generated, only that several issues were grouped under a single entry point at the time.

## The Initial Draft's Trade-offs Are Still Retained

The original discussion was not about a complete design, but about three rough directions.

| Direction | Why It Was Considered at the Time | Costs Left at the Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Collect near blend and publish directly | Callers only needed to know one queue location, with short initial wiring | Batch replay, later consumer hookup, and reference checks might all share state |
| Form a batch first, then hand it to a separate admission point | Publication could be kept separate from sequence checks | There was no answer at the time to who would build the directory or retain replay records |
| Let each consumer interpret the queue contents | Changes were local and appeared to require the least effort | Interpretation of keys, sizes, and backends would be scattered, with no common decision point for duplicate processing |

The initial draft chose the first option as the working direction. It was chosen not because ownership of the publication object had been confirmed, but to let callers start tracing events from a single location. The second option was shelved, but not because it could not be done; there was not enough material at the time to explain how the timing of directory writes corresponded to the timing of reference-count-based eviction. The third option was not adopted because, if multiple consumers independently interpreted the same batch of objects, duplicate processing would leave no way to compare which consumer had already changed the placement relationships.

This decision itself is now outdated, but it explains why, for a period, troubleshooting would first follow `blend_v3.py` to find the queue, then classify whatever could not be found as a publication issue. That route mistook “collection location” for “publication responsibility,” and also mistook “sequence checks” for evidence that “the directory was already complete.” The original assessment is retained to keep the origins of old troubleshooting results understandable, not to present it as a structure confirmed later.

## A Batch Is Not a Single Log Entry

During the later review, the discussion returned to “establish a batch first, then discuss processing order.” The information in a batch cannot be reduced to a vague line of metadata: `backend`, left by the storage side, identifies which storage backend the write came from, while `sizes` corresponds to the size of the written object. The initial draft only noted that “the queue carries metadata” and did not address multiple objects within a batch, so it could not justify letting consumers independently guess what the fields meant.

The draft at the time treated these contents as objects that could be held temporarily before publication, rather than sending a separate notification to every receiver immediately after each object was written. The reason was that sequence checks should operate on an identifiable batch, not merely on scattered keys. This reasoning did not establish that the batch must be created by the blend module; it only argued against the practice of “each consumer reconstructing events from queue fragments on its own.”

The review also left a direct statement of the gap: `The cache event broadcast entry point is not yet available`. This referred to an unfinished implementation that only named the receiving side but had no publication entry point. It does not prove that the broadcaster is in the current file, nor does it mean that the queue itself has completed publication. The initial draft conflated the two, leading later readers to think that finding the queue was enough to finish the check.

## Admission and Directory Updates

The old draft described “admission” as “admission and completion of the directory update.” After review, the decision at the time was to record these two outcomes separately. `EventGate` was used as the name for sequence admission: the first admission of a valid batch was recorded as `admitted`. This result only indicates that the batch passed the admission point; it does not indicate that the placement index has been written, and it cannot substitute for the consumer's processing result.

A duplicate batch was recorded as `duplicate`. The initial draft treated duplicate processing as a side task of queue cleanup on the publishing side, an interpretation that was not retained later. Even if the same batch arrives again, whether its placement changes have already been applied still needs to be determined at the admission boundary; otherwise, “received again” and “changed the directory again” would be recorded as the same phenomenon.

`CacheEventSubscriber` was the name used at the time to distinguish the receiving role. Its original purpose was only to separate the role of receiving batches from the collection queue, not to require every caller to have an independent state machine. The old discussion also raised the idea of consolidating receivers into a single write point, but this was not settled: this decision reached no conclusion on whether receivers should change the directory immediately or retain replay records first.

The initial draft's “single chain” was therefore no longer treated as a complete solution. The narrower decision retained was that publication, sequence admission, and directory writes must not share a single success marker. At the time, this decision only constrained troubleshooting so that one result would not be recorded in place of another; it did not provide a directory interface or specify which call site was responsible for handing a formed batch to the publisher.

## The Old Arrangement for Eviction

The initial draft once described reference-count-based eviction as the natural follow-up to successful publication, and this section is likewise retained as an old arrangement. `FleetEvictionController` was included in the adjacent discussion because it deals with objects that still have references, not with whether the queue is empty. The initial draft suggested first using `filter_unpinned` to select candidate objects, then handing the remaining objects to the eviction controller.

That suggestion was not supported by enough call-site evidence. It can explain why early troubleshooting checked reference state before looking for new events, but it cannot establish that this was the correct processing order. Publication errors, duplicate batches, and unreleased references can occur at the same time; assigning all of them to the eviction controller would only perpetuate the initial draft's conflation.

The intuition that “eviction needs to be observed alongside event processing” was not rejected at the time, but neither was it decided that both must be handled within the same object. If old scripts still run `filter_unpinned` first, that should be regarded as a troubleshooting habit from that stage, not as grounds for concluding that cache event publication has already failed or that a directory update has already occurred.

## Traces of Later Reviews

RCP-223 listed the actual entry point for buffered cache-event as an investigation target, and one point remains unconfirmed in the record. This gap exposes precisely what the initial draft was missing: even if a queue can be found near blend, the reference relationship from collection to publication is still missing. The card did not reclassify the file as the publisher; it only reopened an assessment that had been closed prematurely.

RCP-225 placed sequence admission and reference-count-based eviction in the same round of investigation, with counterexamples added later. Those counterexamples did not automatically produce a new unified design, but they were enough to undermine the claim that “all ordering issues are resolved by the publishing side.” The two cards serve here only as entry points to the review at that time; they did not fill in the directory write order or confirm who retains replay records.

Below is the flow sketch left from the initial-draft period. It describes the processing order that people were trying to connect at the time, not the current responsibility map:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Collection
    Collection --> Batch: Buffering
    Batch --> Admission: Sequence checks
    Admission --> Directory: Envisioned at the time
    Directory --> Eviction: Reference count checks
```

The sketch's only value is to show why the issues were viewed as a single chain at the time: a batch was formed after collection, the directory was considered only after admission, and eviction was then discussed alongside the directory. It does not show later consumer hookup, where duplicate batches are retained, or the actual publication call site; in the initial draft, these gaps were obscured by a single queue concept.

## Retained Decisions and Unresolved Issues

The decision ultimately retained on this page is much narrower than the initial draft: the location where a queue appears can no longer be treated as the owner of the cache event protocol, and `admitted` cannot be treated as synonymous with the directory having been updated. When the publishing side is missing, `The cache event broadcast entry point is not yet available` can be used to identify the gap; duplicate batches are recorded as `duplicate`, and this should not again be used to infer that the directory must have changed.

But this does not mean that the original three directions have converged into a new solution. This old decision still does not settle which call site hands a formed batch to the publisher, how applying directory changes leaves a replay trace, or whether the eviction controller or the receiver observes state first when references have not been released. The initial draft tried to cover these issues with a single queue order; the later review only pointed out that this coverage was unreliable, without replacing it with a complete new chain.

# Caller Integration Dual-State Anomaly Postmortem

This anomaly affected the record for the same object in lmcache · Caller Integration. The entry point showed different current revisions at two points in time. Both sets of content remained available, but they could not be treated as successive states of the same integration run. What first prompted us to stop was not a new integration failure, but a mismatch between the placement directory and the old record: the object referenced by the directory was still there, but the state described in the record had already changed once.

The integration project retained real caller samples, adaptation boundaries, and integration feedback, and had its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. We therefore did not collapse the two states into a single “latest status.” Doing so would erase the context in which the integration feedback arose and could lead later reviewers to believe the old record had never existed.

## Sequence of Events

- On the first check of the entry point, the placement directory did not match the old record. At that point, we could only confirm that the record for the same object had changed. We could not determine whether the directory discrepancy was the cause or a result of the change.
- We then reviewed the entry point at the two points in time and found that each showed a different current revision. The original record had not been replaced, and the recovery page was still retained; the three locations represented different points in time.
- We stopped retrying at that point. Repeating the operation would not join the two records back into a single state and could instead mix later observations into the original samples.
- We subsequently confirmed that the ingest sequence could be restored. Here, “restored” means only that we could return to an ingestion sequence that allowed further checks. It does not mean the payload staging change had been explained.
- The review retraced the original input once and confirmed only the current entry point. Branches that were not reproduced remained open for investigation; we did not turn them into a definite cause on that basis.

The main impact of the anomaly was that the limits of what we could conclude diverged. What the caller saw was not simply an outdated description, but two states of the same object presented through different entry points at different times. Using the newer entry point alone would lose the adaptation context in the old record; continuing solely from the old record would ignore the recovery page that had already appeared. Neither could explain the full situation on its own.

## Changes in Assessment

We initially focused on the placement directory because it was the first place where the discrepancy appeared. We retained that observation but did not elevate it to an attribution of cause. The mismatch between the directory and the old record only indicated that we needed to review the object's record history. It did not prove that a directory change caused the dual state, nor that the adaptation boundary had changed.

The finding that the two points in time showed different current revisions then changed how we handled the issue. We no longer recorded it as “the directory needs correction,” but as records that had not been merged across time: the original record, the recovery page, and the unconfirmed cause remained separate. We retained these three locations so reviewers could distinguish the recovery action that had already occurred, the old state that was still visible, and the payload staging change that remained unexplained.

There had been a tendency to bring observations from adjacent services into the explanation, but the evidence from the incident was insufficient to record them as a cause. That line of investigation was not included in the conclusion. The caller samples and integration feedback collected during integration could establish that the object was indeed in the adaptation chain; they could not establish that adjacent service behavior contributed to this change.

## Recordkeeping After Recovery

After restoring the ingest sequence, we did not backfill the old record or overwrite the initial observation with the recovery page. The original version remains in `docs/adj-lmcache/incidents/lmcache-Caller Integration-Two States for the Same Object.md` because it retains the context of the first placement directory mismatch. The recovery page retains the sequence restoration it describes; the unconfirmed cause remains separate so readers do not interpret “can be restored” as “we know why it changed.”

Stopping retries was also part of the recovery action. Stopping did not mean we had determined that the issue was gone. It was intended to avoid continually creating new ingestion traces while the cause was unknown. The two states already observed were sufficient to support a review; continuing to operate would not automatically explain payload staging.

During review, we accepted only content that could be traced from the original input back to the current entry point. After checking again, the second reviewer still limited confirmation to the entry point and did not expand unreproduced branches into an incident timeline. This limit makes the record look incomplete, but preserves the boundary of what was actually known at the time: the ingest sequence could be restored, while the reason for the payload staging change was still unknown.

## Still Open

No confirmable causal relationship has been established between the payload staging change and the dual state. The available evidence cannot tell us whether it occurred before the old record, between the two revisions, or after recovery. It also cannot establish whether it affected only this object. This gap remains open rather than being filled in with the placement directory discrepancy.

Another incomplete item is the precise chronology of the two points in time. The records confirm that they showed different current revisions in succession, but do not retain enough timestamps to order all the actions. If original timing information becomes available later, it should be attached beside the corresponding record, not rewritten into a seemingly continuous sequence.

The conclusion of this postmortem is therefore narrow: the same object did leave two states, the ingest sequence has been restored, and the cause of the payload staging change remains unconfirmed. The original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause will remain separately retained until new evidence can explain the relationships between them.

4. Check whether the exit actions have been executed; if an action has only been verbally confirmed, leave it as incomplete.

# Caller Integration Test Exit Window Procedure

The exit window covers only caller-side wrap-up for lmcache-client-integration. A checked item means that a record exists or an action is complete at that point, not that the entire release has been approved. Release sign-off remains at the respective maintainer's entry point.

## What to Capture When Opening the Window

- [ ] Locate the entry point for this round of integration testing and confirm that the records still point to `lmcache-client-integration`, not an old page with a similar name.
- [ ] Record the caller's last submitted input and last visible result. If the result came from temporary diagnostics, label it separately; do not mix it with normal integration test results.
- [ ] Mark where the entry point changed. RCPA-009 already noted that statistics from before and after the entry point change cannot be directly subtracted. If the change point is unclear, keep both sets of records without adding a combined total.
- [ ] Check whether `token window` has started. It only defines the observation scope for this round; it is not proof that the caller has exited.
- [ ] If `consumer fan-out` occurs, retain the records for callers still waiting for results, then continue to the next item.

## Exit Actions

1. Verify the exit actions already taken on the caller side. These actions should be traceable in this round's integration test records; do not check them off as complete if all you have is a secondhand account.
2. Record the last visible result and place it near the exit action in the same record. This lets the person taking over see whether the two results belong to the same round without guessing from multiple daily reports.
3. Remove temporary entry points, bypasses, or permissions retained for integration testing after the exit action. Before removing one, confirm that it is not handling calls that have yet to be withdrawn.
4. If integration feedback remains open, record the person taking over and the confirmation time. The supplemental fields in RCPA-007 are the outgoing owner, the person taking over, and the confirmation time; simply writing “continue following up” is not enough.
5. Stop at this step if `webhook mutation` has not appeared. Do not substitute a normal result from the main path.

## Two Common Misinterpretations

Older records once treated the continued presence of a page entry point as meaning that the expiry action was still available. That interpretation is no longer valid: after the expiry action stops working, the entry hint on the page may not have been updated. In that situation, retain the old hint as part of the observed state and continue checking through the existing registration entry point. Do not retroactively change the records from the older round.

RCPA-008 originally proposed maintaining the exit entry point and timeline separately. That was later canceled, and the required information is now maintained through the existing registration entry point. A parallel timeline is therefore no longer required here. The checklist only needs to keep this round's entry point, exit action, and last result together; use only a link when referencing them in a daily report.

A shift handoff is not a substitute for exit verification either. Existing supplemental notes show that the on-duty person could be matched to that round, but the exit entry point had not yet been tried. After the handoff, still check the entry point and actions according to this page. Do not treat the handoff record as a signal to close the window.

## Stop Conditions

Stop further cleanup and retain the records as they stand if any of the following occurs:

- The entry point change cannot be located, so there is no way to tell whether the two results are comparable;
- The caller has confirmed only some of the exit actions;
- `consumer fan-out` still has calls that have not been withdrawn;
- `webhook mutation` is missing;
- The person taking over or the confirmation time is blank.

Stopping does not mean a failure has been established. First retain the last visible result and the actions already performed, then open the next window once the handoff information or entry point details are complete. There is still no shared-environment record for the recovery action, so it cannot be marked as verified here.

The existing material is available at `docs/adj-lmcache/release/lmcache-client-integration-Exit Window Checklist.md`. RCPA-007, RCPA-008, and RCPA-009 can be used to review the original registrations for handoffs, entry point maintenance, and statistical boundaries.

# Caller Integration Testing Exit Window Procedure

The exit window for lmcache-client-integration does not provide release approval. It only keeps three facts together: what exit action the caller took, what result was last observed after that action, and whether any integration feedback still needs to be handed over to the next maintainer. The corresponding maintainer signs off separately on whether the release succeeded.

Before the window opens, first establish where this round's records pick up. The entry point used here is `docs/adj-lmcache/release/lmcache-client-integration-Exit Window Checklist.md`; if the incoming owner arrives from a daily report, an old link, or another information page, first return to this entry point to check the current integration testing records. Identical entry point names do not mean the records belong to the same round, especially since there has already been a case where entry point guidance was not updated when the expiration action occurred.

## Window Opening Records

- [ ] Mark the scope of callers for this round in the integration testing records. The scope describes only callers that have already participated in lmcache-client-integration, not candidates that have yet to integrate.
- [ ] Retain the entry point used at the start of this round. If the entry point changes later, record the point of change near the original location rather than overwriting the old entry point with the new one.
- [ ] Record the original input and the first observed result so they can be used for comparison. Here, the result means the response, status, or integration feedback actually observed by the caller; if none was observed, write that it was not obtained rather than filling in the gap with assumptions.
- [ ] Check whether `token window` has opened. Its purpose is to limit the observation scope of this round's checks, not to signal permission to delete records early.
- [ ] If this round depends on a temporary entry point, bypass, or additional permissions, keep in mind that it is still in use. Do not remove it before exit merely because the main path is working normally.

This section does not require a new master integration testing table. RCPA-008 previously proposed maintaining a separate exit entry point and timeline, but that was later canceled, and the relevant information was returned to the existing registration entry point for maintenance. Window records should follow the existing entry point; daily reports or other pages only need to link to it when referencing it.

## Check the Last Result

Retain one observed result before the exit action and one after it; there is no requirement to copy every attempt into the checklist. At minimum, the records must let the incoming owner see: which caller the result came from, whether it was obtained before or after the exit action, and whether it was affected by an entry point change.

- [ ] If the result comes from the normal integration testing path, keep it together with this round's input and caller feedback.
- [ ] If the conditions were temporarily changed for diagnosis, label this result separately as a post-diagnosis result. It cannot be directly subtracted from the result before the change, nor can it replace the original conditions.
- [ ] If the entry point switches during the window, clearly separate the periods before and after the switch. RCPA-009 recorded that statistics before and after an entry point change cannot be compared directly; without the point of change, do not make trend judgments.
- [ ] If only a secondhand account is available and the actual result has not been seen, retain the scope of that account and leave the status unconfirmed; do not check off the result as verified.
- [ ] If the caller provides rejection or integration failure feedback, retain that feedback in this round's records. Do not delete it because it is not a successful result.

“Last” means only the last result that could be confirmed before this window closes, not that the system will produce no new results afterward. When observation continues in the next round, open a separate record rather than appending a seemingly continuous tail to this round.

## Perform Exit Actions

Exit should begin with actions the caller can still review. First confirm that the target to be exited actually belongs to this round of lmcache-client-integration, then perform cleanup; do not remove integration records with similar names along with it.

1. [ ] Verify the exit actions the caller has already performed. If an action has left no record that can be reviewed, mark it as pending confirmation rather than substituting “notified”.
2. [ ] Check the caller's result again after the action, and record that result immediately next to the action. If there is no result, retain the fact that there is no result.
3. [ ] Check `consumer fan-out`. The main call ending does not mean related calls have stopped; callers still waiting for results must remain within the window.
4. [ ] Only after confirming that related calls no longer use the temporary entry point should you revoke bypasses, temporary permissions, or anything else retained solely for integration testing.
5. [ ] If a cleanup task would change conditions still under observation, stop first. First record that the action has not been performed and why; do not change the sample just to complete the checklist.

“Cleanup complete” is not represented here by a single checkbox. Exit actions, the ending of related calls, and the removal of temporary entry points may be completed at different times. Only by recording a separate result for each can the incoming owner determine whether the window is blocked on the caller, the entry point, or feedback that has not yet concluded.

## webhook Branch

`webhook mutation` is the explicit stop point on this page. If it has not appeared, other normal signals cannot be used to infer that exit is complete.

- [ ] If it has appeared, record which caller result it appeared near, then continue checking related calls and temporary entry points.
- [ ] If it has not appeared, stop closing the window and do not revoke integration testing entry points that this branch may still use.
- [ ] If it has appeared but cannot be matched to a caller in this round, retain the record without treating it as a pass for this round.
- [ ] If only the main path has a result and this branch has none, the main path's result may be retained as the last visible result, but the window status remains incomplete.

Early records described the action to take when this signal had not appeared too briefly, making it easy to read as “check again later”. This is changed here to an explicit stop because subsequent cleanup could deprive the incoming owner of the conditions needed to continue verifying this branch.

## How to Write the Handoff

The supplementary record requirements in RCPA-007 are the outgoing owner, incoming owner, and confirmation time. For an exit window, at minimum record who handed it over, who received it, and which portion of the records the recipient confirms receiving. The handoff does not need to repeat the entire integration testing history; write only the specific actions still incomplete, the location of the last visible result, and the reason for stopping.

- [ ] If there is an incoming owner, specify whether they are taking over entry point verification, caller feedback, related calls, or recovery actions.
- [ ] If there is a confirmation time, place it next to the handoff item; if the time is blank, the window cannot be marked as handed over.
- [ ] Retain a handoff item even when handing over to the same maintainer to continue handling it. This prevents incomplete actions from being disguised as unclaimed old records.
- [ ] If there is only an on-duty handoff and no exit entry point verification, still treat it as incomplete. Previous records have already shown that a match with the person on duty for that round does not mean the exit entry point has been tested.

There are still no results for recovery actions in the shared environment. Do not write “recovery available” for “recovery not triggered”, and do not check off this item just because exit actions worked normally. If recovery records are obtained later, separately specify the caller and window they correspond to; do not backfill them as results already verified at the time of this round.

## Sequence Before Closing the Window

When closing the window, follow the actual dependencies, not the number of checkboxes on the page: first confirm the last visible result, then confirm the exit action, then check `consumer fan-out` and `webhook mutation`, and finally handle temporary entry points and the handoff. If there is no evidence for earlier actions, subsequent cleanup can be paused.

- [ ] This round's entry point and its points of change have been retained.
- [ ] The caller's exit actions are recorded.
- [ ] The last visible result after the action has been retained, or it has been explicitly stated that no result was obtained.
- [ ] Related calls still waiting have been marked.
- [ ] `webhook mutation` has appeared and can be matched to this round, or the window has explicitly stopped at this item.
- [ ] Temporary entry points, bypasses, and permissions are revoked only after confirmation that they no longer handle calls.
- [ ] Incomplete items have an incoming owner and a confirmation time.

Any missing item can stop the window from closing. When stopping, retain the current entry point, the exit actions already performed, and the last visible result; do not invent judgments just to make the records look tidy. If the entry point has changed, the expiration action is no longer valid, or statistics are not comparable, do not go back and rewrite the original records of an old window either.

RCPA-009 are used to review the statistical boundary caused by entry point changes; RCPA-007 are used to supplement handoff information; RCPA-008 retain the background on why a separate exit timeline is no longer being created. They are all supporting entry points for the current checklist and do not replace the records here of this round's exit actions and stop points.

# Integration Route Proposal Not Adopted

This route was ultimately not retained as the integration approach for lmcache-client-integration. This draft is still kept because the objections at the time went beyond “too large a change”: the options being compared, the callers that had not been found, and what would need to be restored on withdrawal were all documented in the same round of discussion. Later reviews of the cards did not turn up enough material to recast the old assessment as a present-day conclusion.

The initial wording reduced the choice to two options: continue along `cache-event batch`, or take `eviction pin` out of the batch path. That framing had its limits. It described only the two destinations identified in the integration draft. It did not establish that they covered all callers, or say which entry point would be switched first if the route were adopted.

## Why a split was considered at the time

The old draft noted that the two sections in the source material had different failure exits. It therefore proposed handling pin separately: batches would still be passed through as before, while pin issues would not be described through the same batch-processing exit. The value of this idea was only that the two failure surfaces could be discussed independently; it did not mean a new interface boundary had been confirmed.

Keeping the batch path also had a clear cost. Callers that continued to look only at batch results would not change their integration because of the draft on this page. But if the split route had already affected the same set of caller samples, maintaining pin separately would create two entry points that needed to stay aligned. The callers then using `namespace reference` had not been identified, so there was no way to determine which adapters would bear that cost.

That gap was never subsequently filled with a confirmed finding. The old document’s “leaning toward a split” was only a working assessment from the meeting, not a scheduling commitment, much less notice of a change to existing calls.

## Constraints before any trial

The draft required both routes to use the same inputs and observation window, changing only the route itself. The purpose was not to get a single green run, but to avoid mistaking input differences for route differences. Without actual caller samples, or with only display labels changed, this comparison could not be replaced.

Another, more specific stopping condition concerned restoration. If exiting could only send callers back to the old entry point, but could not restore the original `event handle`, the split should not continue. This condition is retained here because the concern at the time was not that “the new route looks bad,” but that restoration might be only half complete.

The draft recorded neither a start date nor a handover to a long-term maintainer. The constraints above therefore cannot be described here as a trial that was carried out, and there are no results that establish the split route as better than keeping the batch path.

## Card traces left afterward

RCPA-005 was later used as an entry point for follow-up checks of the recording window for the unadopted proposal.
